name: Quitting smoking / vaping
lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is a practice appearance communities associate with healthier-looking, younger-looking skin and a leaner, fresher look. The face of long-term smokers has a documented pattern, often called smoker's face, that includes a characteristic wrinkle pattern, sagging and a sallow grey skin tone, and people who quit do so partly with the aim of avoiding or slowing these changes.[1]

A 1985 BMJ study by D. Model reported certain facial features in about 46% of continuing smokers but only about 8% of former smokers who had smoked for a decade.[1] Proposed mechanisms include raised matrix metalloproteinases that break down collagen and elastin, narrowed blood vessels that cut oxygen delivery to skin, and oxidative stress.[1] Research on vaping has concentrated on lung and cardiovascular effects rather than skin.[2][3][4]

On looksmaxxing forums, the topic runs in two directions. Some members describe nicotine from vapes as an appetite suppressant and leanmaxxing tool, while others describe quitting as part of a routine to improve skin, stamina and general condition. Reported experiences are anecdotal.[5][6][7]

chain: Less collagen breakdown and better skin oxygenation
Fewer smoker's-face features, healthier colour and tone
angle.text: Smoking is classed as an extrinsic ager of skin, so stopping removes a recurring source of collagen loss, vessel narrowing and oxidative stress. In the 1985 BMJ comparison, the smoker's-face features were far less common in former smokers than in continuing smokers.[1] People also describe quitting as improving skin colour, breathing and training capacity.[8]

paras: Smoking is classed as an extrinsic aging factor. It lowers oxygen delivery to skin, depletes antioxidants such as vitamin C and raises enzymes that break down the structural matrix of the skin, leaving it thinner and more lax.[1] Wikipedia also lists hair loss, gum disease, tooth staining and a higher skin cancer risk among smoking-associated changes.[1]

sections.h: What quitting is reported to change
paras: In the 1985 BMJ study described on Wikipedia, the facial features occurred in about 46% of continuing smokers and 8% of former smokers with a ten-year history, and were absent in non-smoking controls.[1] That comparison is observational; the sources do not state how fast or how completely skin recovers after stopping.

Lung cancer risk is reported to begin falling soon after quitting and to drop by about half after ten years.[11] A T Nation member in a long-running quit thread described being a week in and noticing that his skin had color and breathing was easier.[8]

Vaping is often described by users as a way to stop smoking or to curb appetite. Reviews in medical journals say vaping is not without risk, and that the e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) outbreak of 2019 led to more than 2,800 hospitalizations in the United States.[2][3][4] An American Heart Association scientific statement says cardiovascular and pulmonary effects of long-term use remain under study.[4][12] No study found has measured facial skin changes after stopping vaping.
Randomized trials have tested ways of helping young people stop vaping, including a text-message program for adolescents and a trial of varenicline with counseling in youth who vape.[9][10]

On looksmax.org, threads describe nicotine vaping as an appetite suppressant for cutting weight, with posters writing about leaner faces; other members answer that it irritates their lungs or may affect growth, and some threads record quitting attempts.[5][6][13] A thread asks whether quitting smoking helps rebuild collagen.[14]

No studies found on quitting vaping for appearance. For smoking, one observational study compared facial features of current, former and non-smokers.[1] Randomized trials of vaping cessation measure quitting rates rather than skin outcomes.[9][10]

timeline.event: Model publishes 'Smoker's face: an underrated clinical sign?' in the BMJ.[1]
EVALI outbreak in the United States leads to more than 2,800 hospitalizations.[4]
JAMA publishes a randomized trial of a text-message vaping cessation program for adolescents.[9]
JAMA publishes a randomized trial of varenicline for youth vaping cessation.[10]

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss nicotine in two ways: as a leanmaxxing aid and as something to quit for skin, lungs and stamina.[5][6]

claims.claim: Nicotine vaping suppresses appetite and gives a leaner, hollow-cheeked face
claims.believers: Posters say a vape helped them eat one meal a day or lose around 40 pounds, using a flavored vape against sweet cravings.[5][6]
claims.experts: Reviews describe vaping as linked to lung injury and cardiovascular changes, and say vaping is not without risk.[2][4][12]

claims.claim: Vaping and smoking hurt looks or stunt growth
claims.believers: Members say it makes lungs feel burnt or is bad for bone growth, and some start threads about quitting.[7][13]
claims.experts: The sources found address lung and heart effects of vaping, not growth or facial appearance.[2][4]

claims.claim: Quitting smoking lets skin rebuild collagen
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether collagen can be rebuilt after quitting.[14]
claims.experts: The smoker's-face comparison found the features far less common in former smokers than current ones; how skin recovers over time is not described.[1]

card.summary: Quitting smoking or vaping to slow skin aging; smoker's face is documented, quitting's facial reversal is thinly studied.
card.note: Nicotine cessation: seek medical support if needed.

quick.overview:
Smokers show a characteristic aged look: wrinkles and grey, sallow skin. Some people quit hoping to look younger.

Observational data show the features are less common in former smokers, but reversal is not well established.
quick.mechanism: Smoking raises collagen-degrading enzymes, narrows blood vessels and increases oxidative stress.
quick.risks: Smoking carries major documented harms including cancers, heart and lung disease. Quitting is associated with falling lung cancer risk over years.
